Chapter 4

Building Cohesive Teams

打造有凝聚力的团队

In Chapter 3, we acknowledged that you likely didn’t get this job because things were going smoothly and that, more often than not, engineering leaders step in when something is broken. And nothing is better at breaking teams than chaos.

在第 3 章里，我们承认了一件事：你大概率不是因为一切都顺风顺水才得到这份工作的；更多时候，工程领导者是在某个东西坏掉的时候被请进来的。而要说什么最能搞垮团队，那非混乱莫属。

When Juan joined Splice as its first engineering leader, the team was about to raise a major round of funding and was preparing for explosive growth. From the outside, it looked like liftoff. Inside, it was barely held together: 12 people—5 of which were engineers—fragile engineering fundamentals, and no real team structure. It was just a team of smart but exhausted individuals sprinting toward burnout. That’s not unusual; most leaders don’t inherit a cohesive team. Often, they inherit chaos, drift, and the pressure to fix it—fast.

当 Juan 作为 Splice 的第一位工程领导者加入时，团队正准备融一大轮资、迎接爆发式增长。从外面看，像是即将升空。但里面呢？几乎是勉强粘在一起：12 个人——其中工程师只有 5 个——工程根基脆弱，根本没有真正的团队结构。那只是一群聪明但疲惫的人，在朝着 burnout 冲刺。这并不罕见；大多数领导者接手的都不是一支有凝聚力的团队。他们接手的往往是混乱、漂移，以及“赶紧把它修好”的压力。

You don’t fix that with process. You fix it by rebuilding the team from the inside out. That starts with psychological safety, followed by functionality, and then capabilities. Only once those foundations are in place should you grow.

这种事靠流程是修不好的。你要靠从内到外重建团队来修。起点是心理安全（psychological safety），然后是功能性（functionality），再然后是能力（capabilities）。只有这些地基打好了，你才应该扩张。

This chapter is your roadmap for that journey. And if you’re not stepping into a new team right now, pretend you are. Look at your current team with fresh eyes. What would you see if you’d just inherited it? Where would you start?

本章就是这段旅程的路线图。如果你现在并不是刚接手一支新团队，那就假装自己是。用新鲜的眼光看看你现在的团队。如果你是刚接手它，你会看到什么？你会从哪里开始？

It Starts with Safety

一切始于安全

You walk into the room, and suddenly everything’s a little quieter. People hold their questions a beat longer. They start editing themselves. Everyone’s wondering the same thing: “What does this new leader mean for me?”

你走进房间，突然一切都安静了几分。人们把问题多咽了一拍。他们开始自我审查。每个人心里都在想同一件事：“这个新领导，对我意味着什么？”

That’s not insecurity; it’s a kind of survival instinct. Change can feel threatening, especially for teams that are overworked, have had negative past experiences, or lack information. You can’t drive change if your team feels under threat.

那不是不安全感；那是一种生存本能。变革可能让人感到威胁——尤其是对那些已经超负荷、有过负面经历、或者信息匮乏的团队。如果你的团队感到受威胁，你就推动不了变革。

— 原书第 79 页 —

If you want to fix or improve anything, your first job is to lower the threat level. In case you haven’t read it, Google’s Project Aristotle,1 the company’s massive study of what makes teams effective, found that psychological safety was the number-one factor. It wasn’t intelligence. It wasn’t tenure. It wasn’t tooling. It was safety—the ability to speak up without fear. If your team doesn’t feel safe being honest, you won’t get genuine feedback. You’ll just get silence.

如果你想修好或改进任何事，你的第一项工作就是降低威胁等级。如果你还没读过，Google 的“亚里士多德计划”（Project Aristotle）——这家公司关于“什么造就高效团队”的大规模研究——发现心理安全是排名第一的因素。不是智商。不是资历。不是工具。是安全——能够毫无畏惧地开口说话。如果你的团队觉得说真话不安全，你就拿不到真实反馈；你只会得到沉默。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

When April joined her first PixelCurl team meetings, she noticed the pattern immediately: cameras off, short answers, no one jumping in to help when someone struggled to explain a blocker. She asked, “What have you been struggling with lately?” The chat stayed silent. Finally, a senior engineer unmuted: “Nothing that we can’t handle.” April recognized the self-protection. At the next meeting, she tried something different. She shared her screen showing her chaotic attempt to understand their deployment pipeline and said, “I’ve been here two weeks, and I still can’t figure this out. I watched the recording from last week and got completely lost.” In chat, a junior engineer typed, “lol same—Marcus and Jordan both do it differently and there are no docs.” The floodgates opened. People started sharing frustrations in chat and voice. April didn’t solve anything that day, but she lowered the threat level enough that people felt safe being honest, even over a video call.

April 第一次参加 PixelCurl 的团队会议时，立刻注意到了那个模式：摄像头全关、回答简短、有人费劲解释某个 blocker 时没人跳出来帮忙。她问：“你们最近在为什么发愁？” 聊天框一片沉默。终于，一位资深工程师开了麦：“没什么我们搞不定的。” April 认出了这种自我保护。下一次会议，她换了个做法。她共享屏幕，展示自己试图理解他们部署流水线时那一团乱的样子，然后说：“我来了两周了，还是没搞明白这个东西。我看了上周的录像，完全看迷路了。” 聊天框里，一位初级工程师打出：“哈哈我也是——Marcus 和 Jordan 两个人做法都不一样，而且根本没有文档。” 闸门一下打开了。大家开始在聊天和语音里分享各自的憋屈。那天 April 什么问题都没解决，但她把威胁等级降得足够低，让大家哪怕是在视频会议里也敢说真话了。

To be clear, safety doesn’t mean comfort, and it doesn’t mean coddling. It means creating the conditions where people can operate with honesty, courage, and clarity, without fear of punishment or humiliation. In practice, this looks like the following:

说清楚：安全不等于舒服，也不等于娇惯。它意味着创造一种条件，让人们能够诚实、勇敢、清醒地做事，而不害怕被惩罚或羞辱。在实践中，它长这样：

  • Showing up curious and calm

    带着好奇心和平静出现

  • Protecting your team publicly

    在公开场合保护你的团队

  • Naming the tension, and acknowledging any uncertainties or fears

    说出紧张感，并承认任何不确定性或恐惧

  • Normalizing learning and failure

    让学习和失败成为常态

  • Listening more than you speak (at least at first)

    多听少说（至少在一开始）

If you hold yourself to these conditions as a foundation, you stand a good chance of being able to build an effective and cohesive team.

如果你把这些条件当作基础来要求自己，你就有很大机会建起一支高效、有凝聚力的团队。

1 Google’s Project Aristotle identified psychological safety as the most important factor in team effectiveness. The full findings are available at rework.withgoogle.com.

1 Google 的“亚里士多德计划”将心理安全识别为团队效能最重要的因素。完整研究结果见 rework.withgoogle.com。

Get a Functional Team, Fast

快速让团队运转起来

When you take over a struggling team, the problems are rarely subtle. People are juggling too much, and priorities are shifting weekly. Deadlines are slipping—or worse, being met at the expense of work–life balance and quality. No one’s confident, and everyone’s tired.

当你接手一支挣扎中的团队时，问题很少是微妙的。人们同时在扛太多事，优先级每周都在变。截止日期在滑——更糟的是，有些是靠牺牲工作生活平衡和质量才赶上的。没人有信心，每个人都很累。

In these moments, there’s a temptation to go big—to set a bold new direction, roll out a better process, or fix the culture. But trying to solve everything at once almost always makes things worse.

这种时候，人很容易想搞个大的——定一个大胆的新方向、推一套更好的流程、或者改造文化。但试图一次解决所有问题，几乎总是让事情变得更糟。

So, what should your first milestone be? Get the team doing good work. It doesn’t have to be perfect work, just good enough to keep moving forward. Focus first on stabilization, not optimization. Your goal is to create enough clarity and space for progress to happen without causing new problems. This helps the team get a win and take a breather, while also giving you room to think through the next steps. Functionality is the goal; cohesion and performance come later.

那么，你的第一个里程碑应该是什么？让团队开始做出好的工作。不必是完美的工作，只要好到能继续向前推进就行。先聚焦稳定化，而不是优化。你的目标是创造足够的清晰和空间，让进展能够发生、同时不制造新问题。这能帮团队拿到一场胜利、喘一口气，也给你自己留出思考下一步的空间。功能性是目标；凝聚力和绩效是后来的事。

Understand the Work

理解工作本身

Before you start fixing anything, we encourage you to review the work ahead of the team. Yes, you should talk to your crew and others around the organization, but those accounts will come through a human filter. A feature is a feature. The implementation may vary, but the outcomes should be clear. So, dig into the work—not what’s on the roadmap, not what the strategy doc says, and not what you think the team should be doing. Focus on what they’re actually doing, day to day, task by task, under real-world conditions.

在你开始修任何东西之前，我们建议你先复盘摆在团队面前的工作。是的，你应该和你的人聊、也和组织里的其他人聊，但那些叙述都会经过一层人的滤镜。功能就是功能。实现方式可能各异，但结果应该是清晰的。所以，扎进工作本身——不是路线图上写的、不是战略文档里说的、也不是你认为团队应该做的。聚焦在他们实际在做的事：日复一日、一个任务接一个任务、在真实世界条件下做的那些事。

That means observing the work closely. For example, you could sit in on standup meetings, watch a deploy, or ask someone to walk you through their week. Look at what’s in progress, what keeps slipping, and what’s quietly draining energy. We’ve found that understanding the work is one of the most reliable ways to get a clear picture of a team’s state.

这意味着要近距离观察工作。例如，你可以旁听站会、看一次部署、或者请某个人带你过一遍他一周的工作。看看什么在进行中、什么一直在滑、什么在悄悄消耗精力。我们发现：理解工作本身，是看清团队状态最可靠的方式之一。

If the work seems viable, well scoped, documented, reasonably planned, and generally moving forward, then the next place to look is the team. Are they equipped? Are they skilled and cohesive? Are there dynamics slowing them down? If the work itself is unclear—poorly scoped, with unrealistic expectations or constant pivots—then the problem may lie elsewhere: in planning, dependencies, cross-team agreements, or upstream leadership.

如果工作本身看起来可行、范围清晰、有文档、规划合理、整体在向前走，那下一个要看的就是团队。他们装备齐了吗？他们有技能、有凝聚力吗？有没有什么团队动力在拖慢他们？如果工作本身就不清楚——范围界定糟糕、期望不现实、或者一直在转向——那问题可能在别处：在规划、依赖、跨团队协议、或者上游领导那里。

When a team isn’t performing well, there’s usually some misalignment at the core. And there are always two sides to the story. Consider “The team missed a deadline,” versus “We were given a date without a chance to agree to it.”

当一支团队表现不佳时，核心处通常存在某种错位。而一件事总有两面。想想这个对比：“团队没赶上截止日期”， vs. “他们给了我们一个日期，却从来没给我们机会去同意它。”

— 原书第 81 页 —

Understanding why things are going wrong is often more important than identifying what is going wrong. A missed ship date isn’t the diagnosis; it’s the symptom. The root causes could include capacity issues, skill gaps, planning debt, weak leadership, or a combination of all of these.

理解“事情为什么出问题”，往往比识别“什么出了问题”更重要。错过发布日期不是诊断，它只是症状。根因可能包括产能问题、技能缺口、规划债、软弱的领导力，或者这一切的组合。

Start by making the problems visible. Follow the work, and let it show you what’s actually happening. From there, you can begin mapping patterns and guiding the team with clarity.

从让问题变得可见开始。跟着工作走，让它告诉你实际在发生什么。从那里，你就可以开始绘制模式、并用清晰指引团队。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

April spent her first week at PixelCurl doing precisely this. She reviewed every ticket in flight, attended standup meetings with minimal participation, and watched a complete deployment cycle from planning to production. What she discovered didn’t match what she’d been told in interviews. The roadmap showed a clear focus on new rendering features, but the actual work told a different story: 60% of engineering time was going to support requests from the sales team for custom client integrations. Instead of being tracked as projects, they were handled as “quick favors” that often took weeks. The team was exhausted, not due to a lack of skill, but because they were tasked with building a custom product for each new customer while also pretending to deliver a standard platform. The work made it clear—this wasn’t a team problem; it was a strategy problem that no amount of process improvement could fix.

April 在 PixelCurl 的第一周做的正是这件事。她复盘了所有进行中的 ticket、以最低限度的参与旁听站会、并观察了从规划到生产的完整部署周期。她发现的情况和面试时被告知的对不上。路线图清楚地聚焦在新的渲染功能上，但实际工作讲了另一个故事：60% 的工程时间花在了销售团队提来的、为客户做定制集成的支持请求上。这些请求没有被作为项目跟踪，而是被当作“小忙”来处理，结果常常要花上好几周。团队之所以疲惫，不是因为缺技能，而是因为他们被要求为每一个新客户做一个定制产品，同时还要假装在交付一个标准平台。工作本身说明了一切——这不是团队问题；这是一个战略问题，再怎么改进流程也修不好。

Renegotiate Commitments

重新协商承诺

You will inherit promises you didn’t make. Some of them are buried in backlogs. Some are recorded on a slide from a board meeting six weeks ago. Some were made in good faith under bad conditions, by people who are no longer around. And now those promises are the team’s problem. This is where a lot of new leaders slip. They want to prove they can execute and be seen as dependable, so they protect commitments at the expense of the team. Do not do that.

你会继承一些并不是你做出的承诺。有些埋在待办列表里。有些记在六周前一次董事会的某张幻灯片上。有些是在糟糕的条件下、由已经不在公司的人本着善意做出的。而现在，这些承诺成了团队的问题。很多新领导就在这里栽跟头。他们想证明自己能执行、想被看作可靠的人，于是以牺牲团队为代价去保护那些承诺。别这么做。

There’s a window, right when you take on a new team, where you have permission to make bold decisions. You can ask hard questions, call out broken plans, or pause work or plans. This is trust credit. You haven’t delivered yet, but people are hoping you might be the one who can turn things around.

在你刚接手新团队的那个窗口期，你拥有做大胆决定的特许。你可以问尖锐的问题、指出坏掉的计划、或者暂停某项工作或计划。这是“信任额度”。你还没交付任何东西，但人们希望你可能就是那个能扭转局面的人。

Use that window well. It won’t last forever, but it can buy you the time to stabilize and rebuild. Removing unrealistic milestones might feel like pushing back, but done right, it builds trust. When you advocate for a plan that the team believes in, they start to believe in you. You’re not just protecting them from bad decisions; you’re giving them a chance to succeed. That matters.

好好利用那个窗口期。它不会永远持续，但它能为你争取到稳定和重建的时间。移除不现实的里程碑可能感觉像在顶回去，但做得对，它会建立信任。当你为一份团队真正相信的计划发声时，他们就会开始相信你。你不只是在保护他们免受坏决策的伤害；你是在给他们一个成功的机会。这很重要。

— 原书第 82 页 —

But be careful not to push it just to prove a point. This isn’t about being right; it’s about being effective. If you want to renegotiate, then be convincing. Come with alternatives and data. Present a clear-eyed assessment of risk.

但要小心：不要为了证明自己对而去硬推。这不是关于“正确”，而是关于“有效”。如果你想重新协商，那就拿出说服力来。带着备选方案和数据来。给出一份清醒的风险评估。

In some ways, influence matters more than certainty. However, influence is built on understanding reality. If you want to lead effectively, you must first diagnose where your team actually is before determining where they can realistically go.

在某些方面，影响力比确定性更重要。然而，影响力建立在对现实的理解之上。如果你想有效领导，你必须先诊断团队实际在哪里，然后再判断他们现实地能走到哪里。

Resetting expectations doesn’t mean lowering ambition—it means protecting focus and giving the team room to deliver sustainable progress without burning out or cutting corners on quality. This requires an honest assessment of current capacity constraints and what is genuinely achievable given the team’s context.

重置期望不等于降低雄心——它意味着保护专注、给团队空间去交付可持续的进展，而不必 burnout 或在质量上抄近道。这需要对当前产能约束、以及在团队具体情境下什么是真正可实现的，做一次诚实的评估。

Do this early, before delivery pressure mounts and before morale erodes. When you wait until people are already struggling to hit impossible targets, renegotiation feels like failure rather than smart leadership.

早点做这件事——在交付压力堆积之前、在士气侵蚀之前。如果你等到大家已经在挣扎着够不可能的目标时才做，重新协商就会感觉像失败，而不是明智的领导。

Ask yourself the following questions:

问问自己下面这些问题：

  • Who made this commitment?

    这个承诺是谁做的？

  • Was the team involved?

    团队当时参与了吗？

  • What tools and timeline would we actually need to deliver this?

    要交付这个，我们实际需要什么工具、多长时间？

  • What is the cost of struggling quietly versus renegotiating openly?

    默默硬扛 vs. 公开重新协商，各自的代价是什么？

This is one of your earliest leadership tests: will you uphold the illusion of progress, or create the conditions for real momentum?

这是你最早面临的领导考验之一：你是要维持“在进展”的假象，还是要为真正的势头创造条件？

Remove Blockers

清除障碍

If you want to build trust quickly, then you need to clear a path.

如果你想快速建立信任，那你需要清出一条路来。

Most teams aren’t blocked by big, strategic challenges. They’re blocked by 100 small things that no one’s had the time or authority to fix—for example, a broken staging environment, a flaky deploy, or an approval process that slows everything down. These aren’t side issues; they’re morale killers.

大多数团队不是被宏大的战略挑战卡住的。他们是被 100 件没人有时间或权限去修的小事卡住的——比如一个坏了的预发环境、一个不稳定的部署、或者一个把一切都拖慢的审批流程。这些不是边缘问题；它们是士气杀手。

When you join a new team, one of the best ways to earn credibility is to ask, “What’s slowing you down?” And then, do something about it. That’s leadership.

当你加入一支新团队时，赢得信誉最好的方式之一就是问：“是什么在拖慢你们？” 然后，真的去做点什么。这就是领导力。

You don’t need to fix everything yourself. However, you do need to demonstrate that you’re paying attention and understand the cost of friction. Show that you care about what’s making the work harder than it needs to be. Start with small wins:

你不需要自己把所有事都修了。但你确实需要表明你在关注、并且理解摩擦的代价。展示你在乎那些让工作变得比本来更难的事。从小胜利开始：

  • Identify something that frustrates the team and resolve it within a week (or a day).

    找出一件让团队沮丧的事，在一周内（或者一天内）解决掉。

  • Remove a painful dependency.

    移除一个痛苦的依赖。

— 原书第 83 页 —

  • Cancel a pointless meeting.

    取消一场毫无意义的会议。

  • Rewrite a tool permission that’s been wrong for months.

    改掉一个已经错了好几个月的工具权限。

  • Purchase an inexpensive (e.g., $20/month) tool that the team has needed for a while.

    买一个便宜的（比如 20 美元/月）团队已经需要了很久的工具。

It’s not about the size of the fix; it’s about the message it sends. Removing blockers shows that you’re working with the team, and not just observing them. And more importantly, you’re willing to spend your influence on things that make their work easier. This is how you start shifting the energy and improving the team—not with grand speeches, but with tests that work, resolved issues, and a smoother path forward.

重点不在修复的大小；而在它传递的信息。清除障碍表明你在和团队一起干活，而不只是站在边上观察。更重要的是，你愿意把自己的影响力花在那些让他们工作更容易的事情上。这就是你开始转变团队能量、改善团队的方式——不是靠宏大的演讲，而是靠跑通的测试、被解决的问题、以及一条更顺畅的前进道路。

Get Capacity Under Control

把产能控制住

Most new leaders look at a roadmap and think they’re seeing the work that needs to be done. But capacity isn’t just what’s in the task tracker; it’s everything that’s happening behind the scenes. And if you don’t get close to it early, you’ll mistake disorganization for progress and overload for engagement.

大多数新领导看着一张路线图，就以为自己看到了所有要做的工作。但产能不只是任务跟踪器里的那些；它是幕后发生的一切。如果你不早点靠近它，你就会把混乱误认为进展、把过载误认为投入。

Sometimes, capacity is taken up by untracked tasks:

有时候，产能被一些没被跟踪的任务吃掉了：

  • A founder asking for a “quick change”

    创始人要求“改个小东西”

  • A product manager slipping in a “small tweak”

    产品经理偷偷塞进来一个“小调整”

  • Another urgent issue to resolve

    又一个要紧急解决的问题

  • A detour into a popular new programming language because someone’s curious and motivated

    因为某个人好奇又有干劲，绕路去学一门流行的新编程语言

None of this is unusual, but it adds up—fast. So, it’s important to start with a straightforward question: “Where is the team’s time going?” Don’t aim to shame anyone, but gather the facts.

这些都不罕见，但它们累积起来——非常快。所以，从一个直截了当的问题开始很重要：“团队的时间都花到哪去了？” 目的不是让谁难堪，而是收集事实。

Then get that inbound work under control. All work, whether planned or unplanned, internal or external, needs to be tracked and visible. If it’s not tracked, it can’t be prioritized. And if it can’t be prioritized, the team will focus on whatever seems most urgent or interesting.

然后把那些涌进来的工作控制住。所有工作——无论计划内还是计划外、内部还是外部——都需要被跟踪、可见。如果没被跟踪，就无法被排优先级。而如果排不了优先级，团队就会聚焦在任何看起来最紧急或最有趣的事情上。

Set a basic standard:

设定一个基本标准：

  • All work is visible.

    所有工作都是可见的。

  • All work is prioritized.

    所有工作都被排了优先级。

  • We only work on what matters.

    我们只做重要的事。

And help the team enforce it. Saying no to a founder isn’t easy. Redirecting a well-meaning leader asking for “just five minutes” takes confidence and clarity. So

然后帮助团队把它执行下去。对创始人说不容易。把一个善意地请求“就五分钟”的领导打发走，需要自信和清晰。所以

— 原书第 84 页 —

don’t leave that burden on individual contributors. Give them clear language and the permission to do so. Be proactive, and send a short note to other leaders: “To help the team stay focused and deliver better, we’re routing all new work requests through a shared intake process. This will help us make better trade-offs and protect capacity for what matters most.”

不要把这个负担压在个体贡献者身上。给他们现成的说法、以及这样做的许可。主动出击，给其他领导发一封短邮件：“为了帮助团队保持专注、交付得更好，我们会把所有新的工作请求都走一个统一的收口流程。这会帮我们做出更好的权衡，并把产能保护给最重要的事。”

Then follow through by reinforcing the message and repeating it when people forget. This behavior won’t change overnight, but your consistency will shape expectations.

然后跟进下去：强化这个信息，在人们忘记的时候重复它。这种行为不会一夜之间改变，但你的一致性会塑造期望。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

April implemented this at PixelCurl immediately. The StudioOps team was overwhelmed by interruptions: founders messaging engineers directly on Slack about demo features, product managers reassigning sprint work midweek for “urgent” client requests, and constant context switching. April sent a brief note to leadership, routing all new requests through sprint planning, and then backed it up. When a founder messaged an engineer directly, she gently redirected: “Added this to our intake board for Monday planning. If it’s blocking you before then, let me know and we can discuss trade-offs.” The first few weeks were uncomfortable, but within a month, the team’s velocity increased because they could focus on completing tasks without frequent interruptions.

April 在 PixelCurl 立刻就这么做了。StudioOps 团队被各种打断淹没：创始人在 Slack 上直接给工程师发消息问演示功能、产品经理在周中把冲刺工作改派去做“紧急”客户请求、以及持续不断的上下文切换。April 给领导团队发了一封简短的邮件，把所有新请求都走冲刺规划收口，然后用行动背书。当创始人直接给工程师发消息时，她温和地把方向纠正过来：“我已经把这个加到我们的收口看板上，周一规划时讨论。如果在那之前就挡住你了，告诉我，我们可以权衡一下。”头几周不舒服，但一个月内，团队的交付速度提升了，因为他们可以专注完成任务，而不被频繁打断。

Also, remember that this kind of structure is just a starting point. A rigid intake system might feel restrictive at first, but it’s temporary. Over time, the team should own its priorities and trade-offs. You’re just giving them the clarity and support to get there. Driven people want to do meaningful work. Your job is to help define what meaningful looks like and protect the space to achieve it.

另外记住：这种结构只是一个起点。一个僵硬的收口系统一开始可能感觉很受限，但它是暂时的。随着时间推移，团队应该自己拥有自己的优先级和权衡。你只是在给他们清晰和支持，让他们能走到那一步。有内驱力的人想做有意义的工作。你的工作是帮他们定义“有意义”长什么样，并保护实现它的空间。

Finally, remember to shift the balance. While every team will have some unplanned, reactive, low-leverage work, if that’s all that they’re doing, then they’re just maintaining operations rather than building.

最后，记住要移动这个天平。每支团队都会有一些计划外的、被动反应的、低杠杆的工作，但如果他们做的全是这些，那他们就只是在维持运营，而不是在建设。

Understand Skills, Dynamics, and Performance

理解技能、团队动力与绩效

As everything else is being set, work, flow, and focus start with observing the team. Who does what? Who leads without being asked? Who quietly shoulders more than their share? Who trusts whom? Who avoids whom? Where does energy go, and where does it get stalled?

当其他一切都在安排就位时，工作、流动和专注始于观察团队。谁在做什么？谁不用被要求就主动带头？谁在默默承担超出自己份额的担子？谁信任谁？谁在躲谁？能量流向哪里？又在哪里卡住？

You’re not just here to build a delivery system. You’re here to understand the people inside it. Every team has a map. And we’re not talking about the org chart. We’re talking about the map that is made of trust, influence, capability, and tension. Your job is to learn that map quickly in order to use it effectively.

你来这里不只是为了建一个交付系统。你是为了理解系统里的人。每支团队都有一张地图。我们说的不是组织架构图。我们说的是那张由信任、影响力、能力和张力构成的地图。你的工作是快速学会这张地图，以便有效地使用它。

— 原书第 85 页 —

Talk to everyone: engineers, designers, leads, quiet contributors, recent hires, and people who have been there since the beginning. In these conversations, you’re listening for patterns:

和每个人聊：工程师、设计师、负责人、安静的贡献者、新员工、以及从一开始就在的人。在这些对话里，你在倾听模式：

  • Who fills in the gaps?

    谁在填补缺口？

  • Who never asks for help?

    谁从来不求助？

  • Who’s disengaged?

    谁心不在焉？

  • Who’s stretched too thin to be effective?

    谁被拉得太薄、已经没法高效工作？

The team knows. They’ve already adapted to what works and what doesn’t. Your job is to bring that knowledge to the surface, make sense of it, and act on what matters. And when you see performance issues, don’t wait. If someone is struggling, chances are the rest of the team has noticed. They’re waiting to see whether you will, too—whether you’ll acknowledge it and take action.

团队知道答案。他们已经适应了什么管用、什么不管用。你的工作是把那份知识带到水面上、弄明白它、并在重要的事情上采取行动。而当你看到绩效问题时，别等。如果有人在挣扎，很可能团队其他人早就注意到了。他们在等着看你会不会也注意到——你会不会承认它、并采取行动。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

April faced this with Marcus, a brilliant senior engineer at PixelCurl who worked in total isolation. He dismissed code review feedback, refused to pair with juniors because it “slowed him down,” and had created a section of the codebase that only he understood. The team had adapted around him for months. April knew everyone was watching. She decided to have a direct conversation with him: “Your technical skills are exceptional, but I need you to pair with junior engineers twice a week and engage constructively in reviews. This isn’t optional.” Of course, Marcus pushed back and tested her resolve for three weeks. But she held firm. Eventually, he chose to change his ways rather than leave the company, and six months later became one of the team’s strongest mentors. The junior engineers who’d been watching learned that April meant what she said about team health.

April 在 Marcus 身上遇到过这种情况——Marcus 是 PixelCurl 一位才华横溢的资深工程师，但完全孤岛式工作。他无视代码评审反馈、因为“会拖慢他”而拒绝和初级工程师结对，并且在代码库里划出了一块只有他自己懂的领地。团队已经围着他适应了好几个月。April 知道所有人都在看着。她决定和他直接谈：“你的技术能力非常出色，但我需要你每周和初级工程师结对两次，并建设性地参与评审。这不是可选项。” 当然，Marcus 顶了回来，连续三周测试她的决心。但她立场坚定。最终，他选择改变做法而不是离开公司，六个月后成了团队里最强的导师之一。那些一直在旁观的初级工程师也学到了：April 说到做到——关于团队健康，她是认真的。

You don’t need a process. You need clarity. Be honest and direct. Set expectations and offer support. Don’t let issues linger. Unaddressed issues don’t stay quiet; they turn into bigger problems and slow progress. And they signal to the team that outcomes don’t matter.

你不需要一套流程。你需要清晰。诚实、直接。设定期望、提供支持。不要让问题拖下去。没被处理的问题不会保持安静；它们会变成更大的问题、拖慢进展。而且它们会向团队传递一个信号：结果不重要。

So, be kind and give helpful feedback. Remember: you set the bar. If you allow poor-quality work to slip through, don’t be surprised when that becomes the new standard.

所以，善意一点、给出有帮助的反馈。记住：标准是你定的。如果你让低质量的工作溜了过去，那就别奇怪那成了新标准。

— 原书第 86 页 —

Capacity Is Not Enough; Build Capabilities

光有产能不够；要建能力

While getting a team to be functional is a win, it’s not the end goal. It just means the issues have been addressed, the work is flowing, and people can breathe again. Now you need to help the team grow, but not by adding more people or repeating the same tasks.

让一支团队运转起来是一场胜利，但它不是最终目标。它只意味着问题被处理了、工作在流动、人们能喘口气了。现在你需要帮助团队成长，但不是靠加人、也不是靠重复同样的任务。

This next phase is about building something deeper: capability. Capabilities enable a team to tackle more complex problems without breaking down. It’s what makes progress sustainable and turns a group of people who can deliver into a team that can lead and improve.

下一个阶段是关于建立更深层的东西：能力（capability）。能力让团队能在不崩掉的情况下处理更复杂的问题。它让进展可持续，并把一群“能交付的人”变成一支“能领导、能改进的团队”。

You’re shifting from “Can we deliver this sprint?” to “Can we consistently deliver value, even under pressure?” You’re moving from “Can we execute?” to “Can we improve how we operate, together?” That is what capable teams do.

你正在从“我们这个冲刺能交付吗？”转向“我们能在压力下也持续交付价值吗？”你正在从“我们能执行吗？”转向“我们能一起改进我们的运作方式吗？”这就是有能力的团队做的事。

Capabilities as a Team-Level Tool

把能力作为团队层面的工具

This idea was inspired in part by Camille Fournier’s post on engineering ladders,2 a tool that helped bring structure and fairness to how individual engineers grow. But teams don’t usually get that same clarity. We expect them to improve without ever defining what “better” looks like.

这个想法部分源自 Camille Fournier 关于工程师职级 ladder 的文章——那个工具为单个工程师的成长带来了结构和公平性。但团队通常得不到同样的清晰。我们期望团队改进，却从来没定义过“更好”长什么样。

A capability framework fills that gap. It defines the skills and behaviors that make teams reliable, adaptive, and resilient—how they collaborate, communicate, and respond when challenges arise. Its purpose is guidance, not evaluation. It works as a tool, providing teams with a shared language for what good looks like, a means of self-assessment, and a path for growth together.

能力框架填补了这个空缺。它定义了那些让团队可靠、适应力强、有韧性的技能和行为——他们如何协作、如何沟通、以及当挑战出现时如何应对。它的目的是引导，而不是评估。它作为一个工具起作用：为团队提供一套关于“好长什么样”的共同语言、一种自我评估的方式、以及一条共同成长的路径。

Just like engineering ladders, capability frameworks need structure and care to be useful. It isn’t about creating a checklist; it’s about creating clarity. Here’s how we’ve seen it work:

就像工程师职级 ladder 一样，能力框架需要结构和用心才能有用。它不是为了造一张清单；而是为了创造清晰。下面是我们看到它起作用的方式：

Define team capabilities. Start by naming the essential skills and behaviors that enable effective teamwork. Examples include navigating ambiguity, sharing progress clearly, or managing dependencies. Keep them tight and clear—enough to guide reflection without overwhelming the team.

定义团队能力。从命名那些让高效协作成为可能的关键技能和行为开始。例子包括：在模糊中航行、清晰地分享进展、或者管理依赖。保持精简、清晰——足够引导反思，但不至于把团队淹没。

2 Fournier’s post offers a framework with structured levels and expectations for individual engineer growth, helping create transparency in career progression within engineering organizations.

2 Fournier 的文章提供了一个带结构化层级和期望的框架，用于单个工程师的成长，帮助在工程组织内创造职业发展的透明度。

— 原书第 87 页 —

Assess team effectiveness. Let teams evaluate how they’re doing against those capabilities. Use structured conversation and input from partners, not just gut feelings. This process is gathering actionable insights, not assigning grades.

评估团队效能。让团队对照这些能力评估自己做得怎么样。用结构化对话和来自伙伴的输入，而不只是直觉。这个过程是在收集可行动的洞见，不是在打分。

Identify areas for improvement. Most teams won’t be strong across the board. That’s fine. Use the assessment to focus the team’s energy. What’s dragging them down? What limits trust, delivery, or learning? Pick a few areas to improve.

识别改进领域。大多数团队不会在所有方面都很强。那没关系。用评估来聚焦团队的能量。什么在拖他们后腿？什么在限制信任、交付或学习？挑几个领域来改进。

Provide a path to grow. Each capability should have clear examples of success and observable behaviors. Provide the team with concrete guidance to aim for. The goal is progress and momentum, not perfection.

提供成长路径。每项能力都应该有清晰的成功范例和可观察的行为。给团队提供具体的、可以瞄准的指引。目标是进步和势头，不是完美。

High-capability teams don’t just work more. They work more effectively, with less conflict, stronger trust, and greater impact.

高能力团队不只是干得更多。他们干得更有效——冲突更少、信任更强、影响更大。

What Great Teams Do

伟大的团队做什么

Enough with frameworks—let’s get specific. What exactly do capable teams do differently in practice?

框架说够了——让我们具体一点。在实践中，有能力的团队到底哪里做得不一样？

We’ve identified seven core capabilities that distinguish the teams that deliver from the teams that get stuck. These aren’t personality traits or abstract ideals. They are observable behaviors that can be discussed and improved. Not all teams need to excel at everything at once, but high-performing teams eventually build strength across all capabilities.

我们识别出了七项核心能力，它们把“能交付的团队”和“卡住的团队”区分开来。这些不是人格特质或抽象理想；它们是可观察、可讨论、可改进的行为。不是所有团队都需要一下子在所有方面都出色，但高绩效团队最终会在所有能力上都建立起实力。

Use this as a diagnostic tool. Where is your team strong? Where are they struggling? What’s the next thing worth focusing on?

把它当作一个诊断工具。你的团队哪里强？哪里在挣扎？下一个值得聚焦的是什么？

They Turn Ambiguity into Action

他们把模糊转化为行动

Most teams are handed vague goals and unclear priorities. The difference is how they respond. Strong teams don’t wait around for perfect clarity. They ask focused questions, connect their work to actual customer problems and business outcomes, and propose direction rather than waiting for it to arrive fully formed.

大多数团队被递到手里的是模糊的目标和不清楚的优先级。区别在于他们如何回应。强的团队不会坐等完美的清晰降临。他们问聚焦的问题、把自己的工作和真实的客户问题与业务结果连起来、并主动提出方向，而不是等方向完整地从天上掉下来。

When a project manager says, “We need to improve onboarding,” a capable team responds with, “Are we trying to reduce drop-off in the first session, or increase activation by day seven? Those are different problems.”

当一个项目经理说“我们需要改善上手流程”时，有能力的团队会回应：“我们是想减少第一次会话的流失，还是想在第 7 天前提升激活率？那是两个不同的问题。”

They clarify early, get stakeholder feedback before they’re too far down a path, and make sure everyone understands not just what they’re building, but why it matters.

他们尽早澄清、在走得太远之前拿到干系人的反馈、并确保每个人不仅理解自己在造什么，还理解为什么它重要。

— 原书第 88 页 —

A team that can’t do this will spin for weeks building something important-ish. A team that can do this will define measurable goals, connect them to the company strategy, and move forward with confidence even when things are uncertain.

做不到这一点的团队会原地打转好几个星期，造一个“大概有点重要”的东西。而能做到的团队会定义可衡量的目标、把它们和公司战略连起来、并在事情不确定时也充满信心地向前走。

They Communicate Relentlessly (and Don’t Make People Chase Them)

他们持续沟通（而不是让别人追着问）

Good teams share progress consistently. You don’t have to chase them down to know where things stand. They share status early and often and surface blockers before blockers become crises. They maintain predictable channels: weekly updates, standups that highlight risk, and Slack threads that document project progress. When they need help, they ask for it with enough context that someone can actually provide support.

好的团队持续分享进展。你不需要追在他们后面问情况。他们早分享、常分享，在 blocker 变成危机之前就把它暴露出来。他们维持可预测的渠道：周报、突出风险的站会、以及记录项目进展的 Slack 串。当他们需要帮助时，他们提问时会带上足够的上下文，让别人真的能提供支持。

Here’s the test: can someone outside your team explain what you’re working on and why? If not, the team isn’t communicating enough.

这里有个测试：团队之外的人能解释你们在做什么、以及为什么吗？如果不能，说明团队沟通得不够。

We’ve seen teams go silent for three weeks, only to surprise everyone with “actually, we’re behind.” That’s not a communication problem; it’s a trust issue. Compare that to teams that raise issues early on in standup meetings: “We hit an unexpected dependency with Platform. Can we renegotiate the timeline? We propose pushing the launch back one sprint.” The outcome will be the same, but they show different levels of capability.

我们见过团队沉默三个星期，然后突然给大家一个惊喜：“其实，我们落后了。”那不是沟通问题；那是信任问题。对比一下那些早早在站会上把问题提出来的团队：“我们和 Platform 团队遇到了一个没预料到的依赖。能重新协商时间线吗？我们建议把发布往后推一个冲刺。”结果可能一样，但它们展现出的能力水平完全不同。

The best teams also make the purpose of their work clear—not just to leadership, but to the rest of the company so that people understand why the work matters.

最好的团队还会把工作的目的讲清楚——不只是对领导，而是对公司里其他人，好让大家理解为什么这件事重要。

They Manage Dependencies Without Drama

他们管理依赖，而不搞戏剧化

No team works in a vacuum. Capable teams know this and plan for it. They track cross-team dependencies proactively. They communicate with other teams directly, early, and clearly. When something breaks down, they collaborate to fix it before escalating. And when they do escalate, they do it to clarify ownership or get an executive decision, not to assign blame or cover their own reputation.

没有团队是在真空里工作的。有能力的团队知道这一点，并为此做计划。他们主动跟踪跨团队依赖。他们直接、尽早、清晰地和其他团队沟通。当事情出问题时，他们先协作修好它，再考虑升级。而当他们真的升级时，升级的目的是厘清归属、或者拿到一个高管决策，而不是为了甩锅、或者保全自己的名声。

Weak teams get blocked and then shrug: “We can’t ship because Team X didn’t deliver their API.” Strong teams see that coming two weeks out, raise it in planning, and work with Team X to either derisk it or adjust scope. They maintain shared accountability for shared outcomes.

弱的团队被卡住然后耸耸肩：“我们发不出去，因为 X 团队没交付他们的 API。”强的团队在两周前就看到了这件事、在规划会上提出来、并和 X 团队一起要么降低风险、要么调整范围。他们对共同的结果承担共同的责任。

If your team is constantly surprised by dependencies, or if they treat other teams like ticket systems instead of partners, you’ve got work to do here.

如果你的团队总是被依赖“惊喜”到，或者他们把其他团队当 ticket 系统而不是伙伴，那你在这块还有工作要做。

— 原书第 89 页 —

They Execute with Discipline, Not Heroics

他们靠纪律执行，而不是靠英雄主义

Capable teams ship predictably—not because they work harder, but because they plan better. They understand their capacity and don’t overcommit. They adjust scope and timelines based on what’s actually happening, not what they wish were happening.

有能力的团队可预测地交付——不是因为他们更拼命，而是因为他们规划得更好。他们理解自己的产能，不超额承诺。他们根据实际在发生的事调整范围和时间线，而不是根据他们希望发生的事。

They refine their process continuously, tweaking standups, improving tooling, and running retrospectives that lead to actual changes.

他们持续打磨流程：调整站会、改进工具、开能带来真实改变的复盘会。

The goal isn’t to ship faster, but more sustainably, at a cadence that’s observable and repeatable. When a team says, “We need to double our headcount to hit our commitments,” that’s usually a sign that they’re operating without discipline. A capable team would instead say, “We’re paced to 70% load and shipping every two weeks. We’re iterating on our retrospectives to reduce rework and improve flow. If priorities expand, let’s discuss scope trade-offs.”

目标不是发得更快，而是更可持续——以一种可观察、可重复的节奏。当一个团队说“我们需要把人头翻倍才能兑现承诺”时，那通常说明他们在没有纪律地运作。而一个有能力的团队会说：“我们按 70% 的负载节奏走，每两周交付一次。我们在迭代复盘来减少返工、改善流动。如果优先级扩大了，我们来讨论范围上的取舍。”

Execution is about finding a rhythm that works for your specific team.

执行，是找到一种适合你这支特定团队的节奏。

They See Risk Coming and Know How to Respond

他们预见到风险、并知道如何应对

Things will go wrong. The question is whether your team is ready when they do. Resilient teams identify risks early. They build monitoring that actually catches problems before customers notice, and they have incident protocols that are both documented well and practiced. When something breaks, they respond quickly and calmly—informing the right people, sending frequent status updates, and keeping stakeholders up-to-date.

事情总会出问题。问题是：当它们出问题时，你的团队准备好了吗？有韧性的团队早早识别风险。他们建的监控是真的能在客户察觉之前抓住问题的，他们的事故预案既写好了、也演练过。当东西坏了，他们快速而冷静地响应——通知对的人、频繁发状态更新、让干系人保持知情。

After the incident, they run a neutral assessment and actually implement the follow-up items, using incidents as opportunities to improve, not as blame exercises. Let’s contrast two scenarios:

事故之后，他们做中立的复盘、并且真的把跟进项落地——把事故当作改进的机会，而不是甩锅的演练。让我们对比两个场景：

Team A. They find out something is broken only when a customer posts on social media about it. They scramble, and no one is sure who should be responding. Updates trickle out inconsistently.

A 团队。他们直到有客户在社交媒体上发帖才知道东西坏了。他们手忙脚乱，没人确定谁该响应。更新零零散散、口径不一。

Team B. Their monitors flag an issue at 2:00 a.m. The on-call engineer pages the appropriate backup. They follow their runbook and resolve the issue within 40 minutes and post a detailed incident report by the end of the day.

B 团队。他们的监控在凌晨 2 点标记了一个问题。值班工程师呼叫了合适的备份。他们按预案在 40 分钟内解决了问题，并在当天结束前发了一份详细的事故报告。

Both teams had an outage, but only one of them was ready for it.

两个团队都经历了一次宕机，但只有其中一个是为此做好了准备的。

They Invest in Team Health (Because It’s Not Optional)

他们投资于团队健康（因为这不是可选项）

Healthy teams don’t just deliver; they sustain themselves. They onboard new people with intention. For example, every new teammate could be assigned a buddy, a 90-day plan, and ample opportunities to ask questions without feeling stupid. Leaders that invest in team health will create working agreements and actually revisit them when the team changes. They support knowledge sharing, such as documentation, pairing, and demos, and they build psychological safety so people can give and receive feedback without feeling like they’re walking on eggshells.

健康的团队不只是交付；他们能自我延续。他们有意识地帮新人入职。例如，每个新同事可以被分配一个伙伴、一份 90 天计划、以及充足的、问问题不会觉得自己蠢的机会。投资于团队健康的领导会建立工作协议，并在团队变化时真的回头审视它们。他们支持知识分享——比如文档、结对、演示——并建立心理安全，让人们能给出和接收反馈，而不用感觉自己如履薄冰。

— 原书第 90 页 —

Critically, they make space for recovery. Not just after intense periods, but as a regular practice: retrospectives that lead to action, time to pay down tech debt, and permission to say “I’m at capacity” without fear of being seen as uncommitted.

关键是，他们为恢复留出空间。不只是在紧张期之后，而是作为一种常规实践：能带来行动的复盘会、偿还技术债的时间、以及说“我已经满负荷了”而不必担心被看作不投入的许可。

When new people join and it takes them two weeks just to figure out how to run the app locally because nobody has time to help, that’s a team health problem. When burnout is normalized, that’s a team health problem. When only the loudest voices are heard, that’s a team health problem. You can’t ship your way out of these issues.

当新员工加入后，因为没人有时间帮忙，他们要花两周才搞清楚怎么在本地跑起来 app——那就是团队健康问题。当 burnout 被常态化时——那就是团队健康问题。当只有最大声的人被听到时——那就是团队健康问题。你没法靠多交付来摆脱这些问题。

They Connect Effort to Outcomes (and Know When to Stop)

他们把努力和结果连起来（并知道何时停下）

Progress isn’t just about movement, but about impact. Strong teams tie their work to measurable business outcomes. They prioritize based on what matters, not just what’s urgent or interesting. They reflect regularly on whether their work is actually achieving results. They celebrate progress that benefits users and the business, rather than simply noting that “we shipped five things.” This is the capability that separates the teams that stay busy from the teams that drive results.

进展不只是关于动起来，而是关于影响。强的团队把自己的工作绑在可衡量的业务结果上。他们根据什么重要来排优先级，而不只是根据什么紧急或有趣。他们定期反思自己的工作是否真的在产生结果。他们庆祝那些让用户和业务受益的进展，而不是简单地记一笔“我们发了五个东西”。正是这项能力，把“一直很忙的团队”和“驱动结果的团队”区分开来。

A team that says “We shipped five features this sprint,” might be working hard, but a team that says “We launched onboarding improvements that reduced drop-off by 12%, putting us ahead of our Q3 engagement goal,” is working with purpose. It’s the difference between outputs and outcomes, between doing things and doing things that matter.

一支说“我们这个冲刺发了五个功能”的团队，也许很努力；但一支说“我们上线了上手流程的改进，把流失率降了 12%，让我们领先于 Q3 的用户参与度目标”的团队，是带着目标在工作。这就是产出和结果的区别，是“做事”和“做重要的事”的区别。

All of these capabilities are essential for long-term success. But you don’t need to be excellent at all of them on day one. Start by assessing where your team is strong and where they’re struggling. Pick one or two areas to focus on, and build from there. High-capability teams perform better, with less conflict, more trust, and greater impact.

所有这些能力对长期成功都至关重要。但你不需要在第一天就在所有方面都出色。从评估团队哪里强、哪里在挣扎开始。挑一两个领域聚焦，然后从那里建起来。高能力团队表现更好——冲突更少、信任更强、影响更大。

Growing Without Losing the Plot

成长但不跑偏

Once the capacity of a well-run team becomes the limiting factor, you’ve earned the right to grow. This isn’t because things are chaotic or someone’s asking for more hands. It’s because your team is focused, capable, and delivering—you’ve hit the edge of what’s possible without new energy or skill. That’s when it’s time to expand the crew.

当一支运转良好的团队的产能成为瓶颈时，你就挣到了扩张的权利。这不是因为事情混乱、或者有人在要更多人手。这是因为你的团队专注、有能力、在交付——你已经摸到了“不加新能量、不加新技能”情况下的天花板。那就是时候扩队伍了。

But growth isn’t linear. Adding people doesn’t automatically increase velocity. A new teammate should bring more than just additional output; they should broaden the team’s strengths and open space for new challenges and possibilities. The best additions expand what the team can take on, while maintaining speed.

但成长不是线性的。加人不会自动提升速度。一个新同事应该带来的不只是额外的产出；他们应该拓宽团队的强项、为新的挑战和可能性打开空间。最好的补充是：在保持速度的同时，扩大团队能承接的范围。

A capable team should develop its members as it grows. This is also the moment to think about who gets to grow with you. If your team is healthy, stable, and skilled, it

一支有能力的团队应该在成长的同时发展它的成员。这也是思考“谁能和你一起成长”的时刻。如果你的团队健康、稳定、有技能，它

— 原书第 91 页 —

can become a platform for developing others. That means making space for people earlier in their careers who bring curiosity, fresh perspectives, and a hunger to learn. Growth works in both directions. As junior or mid-level engineers gain confidence, senior team members also develop—through mentoring, modeling, and reinforcing what they know. Growth becomes mutual. The team deepens as it expands.

就能成为一个发展他人的平台。这意味着为职业生涯早期的人腾出空间——他们带来好奇心、新鲜视角和对学习的渴望。成长是双向的。当初级或中级工程师获得信心时，资深团队成员也在成长——通过辅导、示范、以及巩固他们已知道的东西。成长变成互相的。团队在扩张的同时变得更深厚。

From Supporter to Supported

从支持者到被支持者

As the team grows, your job changes. You move from supporting a group to being supported by one. You stop managing every detail and start reinforcing direction. You focus less on execution and more on clarity, cadence, and culture. Before, you led by proximity. Now, you lead through leverage. This is achieved through:

随着团队成长，你的工作变了。你从支持一个群体，变成被一个群体支持。你不再管理每个细节，而是开始强化方向。你更少关注执行，更多关注清晰、节奏和文化。以前，你靠近距离领导；现在，你靠杠杆领导。这通过以下方式实现：

  • Systems that support the work

    支撑工作运转的系统

  • People who carry the standard

    扛起标准的人

  • Trust that’s been earned and extended

    挣来并被延伸出去的信任

It’s a quiet shift, but it’s real. You can’t lead the same way with 5 people and with 20—and you shouldn’t try.

这是一个安静的转变，但它是真实的。你不能用带 5 个人的方式去带 20 个人——你也不该试。

You Make Yourself Replaceable

让自己变得可替代

A healthy team shouldn’t need you every day. That’s not a problem; it’s the goal. Taking time off shouldn’t feel risky. Being out of the loop shouldn’t stall progress. If your absence breaks the system, you haven’t built a system—you’ve built dependency. Sustainable leadership means building something that works without constant oversight. That’s when real growth becomes possible. You can start looking further ahead—coaching instead of fixing, guiding instead of directing. And the team? They step up. Sometimes, a tech lead starts shaping strategy. Sometimes, a senior individual contributor starts mentoring others. Sometimes, someone simply sees a gap and fills it before you even notice.

一支健康的团队不应该每天都需要你。那不是问题；那是目标。休假不应该感觉像冒险。不在圈内不应该让进展停摆。如果你的缺席会让系统崩掉，那你建的不是一个系统——你建的是依赖。可持续的领导力意味着：建一个不需要持续盯着也能运转的东西。那时真正的成长才成为可能。你可以开始看得更远——教练式而不是修东西式，引导式而不是指挥式。而团队呢？他们会站出来。有时候，一个技术负责人开始塑造战略。有时候，一个资深个体贡献者开始辅导别人。有时候，就是有人看到了一个缺口、在你还没注意到之前就把它填上了。

You Scale the Culture, Too

你也要把文化规模化

When your team is small, culture spreads naturally. People learn how things work just by being present. But as you grow, that organic transmission breaks down. Culture isn’t fixed; it evolves with every new hire, process, and challenge. The question isn’t whether your culture will change—it’s whether you’ll guide that change or let it happen by accident.

当团队还小时，文化是自然传播的。人们只要在场就能学会事情怎么做。但随着你长大，那种有机的传递会瓦解。文化不是固定的；它随着每一次新招聘、每一个新流程、每一个新挑战而演进。问题不在于你的文化会不会变——而在于：你会引导那个变化，还是让它意外发生。

Without intentional effort, culture fragments. New people bring different assumptions. Teams develop their own ways of working. The original intent gets diluted or

没有有意识的努力，文化就会碎裂。新人带来不同的假设。团队发展出自己的工作方式。最初的意图被稀释，或者

— 原书第 92 页 —

lost entirely. What felt natural and obvious when you were a team of 10 becomes unclear and inconsistent at 50.

完全丢失。当你还是 10 人团队时感觉自然、理所当然的东西，到了 50 人时就变得模糊、不一致了。

Scaling culture intentionally means:

有意识地把文化规模化，意味着：

  • Team agreements that evolve deliberately

    经过审慎演进的团队协议

  • Onboarding that explains the “why” behind how you work

    讲清楚“为什么这样工作”的入职过程

  • Stories that preserve decision-making principles across generations of employees

    在一代代员工之间保存决策原则的故事

  • Written norms that help new people understand and uphold what matters

    帮新人理解并坚守重要之事的书面规范

  • Values that stay visible in daily choices as the company transforms

    在公司转型时仍在日常选择中可见的价值观

Culture is never “done”; it’s always evolving. You must shape what it becomes, not assume it will stay aligned on its own. There’s nothing wrong with the evolution of culture, but behavior often changes faster than the words written by founders in the early days. If you don’t tend to culture as you grow, you risk ending up with a company that operates in ways you never intended.

文化永远不会“完成”；它永远在演进。你必须塑造它成为什么样子，而不是假设它会自己保持一致。文化演进本身没什么错，但行为的变化往往比创始人早期写下的那些话要快。如果你在成长时不照管文化，你就有风险最终得到一家公司——它的运作方式完全不是你想要的。

The Bottom Line

底线

Grow when you’re ready, not just when you’re allowed. Hire people who bring fresh energy, not just more capacity. Create space for others to grow, not just deliver. And remember: your goal isn’t to lead forever; it’s to build a team that can operate and make decisions independently of you.

在你准备好的时候再成长，而不只是在被允许的时候。招那些带来新鲜能量的人，而不只是更多产能的人。为别人的成长创造空间，而不只是为交付创造空间。记住：你的目标不是永远领导下去；而是建一支能独立于你运转、独立做决策的团队。

Conclusion: From Chaos to Cohesion

结语：从混乱到凝聚

Most engineering leaders don’t step into high-performing teams. They step into teams under pressure, overloaded, under-supported, and unsure of what’s coming next. This chapter has served as a roadmap for transitioning from chaos to cohesion—not through grand speeches or sweeping changes, but by undertaking the quiet yet essential work of creating safety, stabilizing flow, building capability, and scaling with intention. The hardest part of this job is creating the conditions where people can succeed together. That means making the team functional before it’s fast, capable before it’s big, and trustworthy before it’s impressive.

大多数工程领导者接手的都不是高绩效团队。他们接手的是承压的、过载的、支持不足的、不知道下一步会发生什么的团队。本章是一份从混乱走向凝聚的路线图——不是靠宏大的演讲或一刀切的变革，而是靠那些安静却必要的工作：创造安全、稳定流动、建立能力、有意识地规模化。这份工作最难的部分，是创造让人们能共同成功的条件。这意味着：先让团队能运转，再让它跑得快；先让它有能力，再让它变大；先让它值得信任，再让它令人印象深刻。

If you do that well, you won’t just lead a better team, you’ll build one that doesn’t depend on you to thrive. When you’re ready to go deeper, others have written far more eloquently and in more detail about managing teams and scaling leadership.

如果你做得好，你不只是领导一支更好的团队，你会建一支不需要靠你才能蓬勃生长的团队。当你想深入下去时，关于团队管理和领导力规模化，其他人已经写得远比你更雄辩、更详尽了。

In Chapter 5, we’ll delve deeper into setting direction for your team.

在第 5 章，我们会更深入地探讨如何为你的团队设定方向。
